newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania in new Ukraine talks vital for NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Romania in new Ukraine talks vital for NATO entry.

text.p: Romania launches a fresh round of talks this week in neighbouring Ukraine on concluding a thorny post-communist treaty seen as vital to bolster its case for early NATO admission.

Discussions opening in Kiev on Tuesday are the ninth round of talks long blocked by disputes rooted in the run-up to World War Two but now apparently dominated by Black Sea border delineation and possible oil and gas rights.

But Romania's delegation will be spurred by exhortations from the West that its longshot bid for early NATO membership -- its main foreign policy objective -- can go nowhere without a treaty similar to one concluded last year with Hungary.
"We understand the necessity of speeding up treaty talks with Ukraine and hope to finalise them by the spring," Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea told foreign journalists.

"We will do everything possible to get Romania into the first wave of admissions, which could be the last. We also have good relations with Poland. We want to forge a three-pronged pole of stability including Romania, Ukraine and Poland."

French President Jacques Chirac said during a visit to Romania last week that he backed its early entry to NATO alongside favourites Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic. But he called for quick action on the treaty with Ukraine.
President Emil Constantinescu said Romania was prepared to make "historic sacrifices" in its dealings with Ukraine to press ahead with NATO membership.

Romanian officials acknowledge that their longstanding call for Ukraine to atone publicly for the Soviet Union's 1940 seizure of large chunks of Romanian land under the Nazi-Soviet pact is no longer the main issue.
Attention has shifted to Serpent Island, an outcrop off both countries' coast. Ukraine claims the island, ceded to Moscow by Communist Romania in the 1950s, as its own.
Several hundred Ukrainian troops maintain a rotating presence on the island, but the real issue is linked to sea borders on a continental shelf being explored for oil and gas.
Ukraine, which jealously guards its newfound sovereignty after three centuries of rule from Moscow, calls for an end to ambiguity in borders with Romania.

"We want the pact to contain unconditional recognition by both sides of land and sea borders and an agreement to make no territorial claims now or in future," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko told Reuters in Kiev.
"If during this round of talks we can resolve these problems, including the future delineation of territorial waters, this will not take a great deal of time."

Unlike Russia, Ukraine says it has no objections to NATO expansion and has even hinted it might one day be able to join the Alliance itself. Moldova, sandwiched between Ukraine and Romania, also offers no opposition to an expanded NATO.
Romania says NATO enlargement depends on the Alliance reaching a separate accord with Russia, which Moscow says is necessary to safeguard its own security interests.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, speaking in Norway said that progress had been made in NATO enlargement talks in Brussels at the weekend.
Ciorbea told journalists he hoped Bucharest could also move forward soon on its own treaty with Russia, also affected by Romanian grievances over the wartime loss of its territory.
"We never intended to have hostile relations with Russia," he said. "We have repeated over and over again that our desire to join NATO is not a hostile gesture against Russia."
